General.Description:
In 1937, women were not supposed to fly commercial aircraft. They were certainly not supposed to do so alone, across the Atlantic, in an open-cockpit biplane, during a storm system that grounded every male pilot in the region. Amelia Hartley did it anyway, and when she landed in Lisbon twenty-seven hours later she became the most famous aviator in Britain — for approximately two weeks, before the newspapers moved on to something else.

Dominic Featherstone spent a decade reconstructing Hartley's extraordinary life from private correspondence, RAF training records, wartime service files, and interviews with her surviving family members. What he found was a woman whose public fame obscured both the depth of her achievement and the systematic ways in which that achievement was minimised, co-opted, and eventually forgotten.

Wings of Change is biography as reclamation. Hartley was not only a pilot of exceptional skill — she was a flight instructor, an engineer, a tireless advocate for women in aviation, and a wartime ferry pilot who logged more hours than most of her male counterparts. She was also funny, sharp, and magnificently unimpressed by authority.

Featherstone restores her to the prominence she deserves. A beautiful and vital book.
